h1: Convert a Link to Video From the Product Page
lead: A URL to video run turns a public product page into a spoken ad. Paste that page, and the lunch box photo there stays the product in the clip.

benefits_h2: Why a URL to Video Starts From the Listing

benefits.d: Paste the lunch box page once and the clip starts from that page. The picture on the public page is the one that enters the project, so you do not re-upload the lunch box photo.

benefits.t: Scripts in the Languages You Sell
benefits.d: The script comes back with the lunch box page, and it can use a fact the listing already states. If you also sell that lunch box in French, the draft can be written in French.

benefits.t: Actors That Can Carry an Ad
benefits.d: Use one actor for the lunch box and the next color so the two ads look like one shop. The library has 53 AI actors.
The lunch box clip can go out as a paid ad or a listing video once you approve it. A 15-second clip is 60 credits, and a 6-second cut is 24. You see that cost before it runs.
You can change the voice after the draft comes back. The edit still says what the lunch box page says, and you do not start a new project.

steps_lead: A public product page for the lunch box is the only link you need.

faq.q: How does a shop get a clip from a listing?
faq.a: Paste the public product page, pick an AI actor, approve the script, and download the clip. The photo on that page is the product in the file.

faq.q: Is there a charge to start from a link?
faq.a: Yes. Starter is $24.50 a month for 200 credits, Pro is $35 for 300, and Premium is $63 for 600. A video spends 24, 40, 60, or 120 credits for 6, 10, 15, or 30 seconds. You see the cost before it runs, and a failed render returns those credits.

faq.q: What kinds of clips can a link become?
faq.a: A listing video, a product demo, a paid ad, or a social clip. Each one can use the photo and the facts already on that public page.
Yes. Shops use it for ads, product pages, and social posts. You approve the script before the file is downloaded.

faq.q: Can I change the drafted script?
faq.a: Yes. Read the script, change any line that does not match the listing, and then render. The wording stays yours.

faq.q: Which file types and frames are available?
faq.a: You download a video file. Frames are 9:16, 1:1, 16:9, 4:3, and 3:4. Lengths are 6, 10, 15, or 30 seconds.

faq.q: What happens after I paste a product page?
faq.a: The photo and the written facts come in from that page. You get a draft script, then you pick an actor and a voice before the clip is made.
No. You can still open the editor if you want to trim the clip, change the music, or fix a line. A first clip does not require a timeline.
Public product pages a shopper can open without logging in. A locked page, a private file, or a page with no product photo will not supply the picture.

faq.q: Why bother starting from the listing?
faq.a: The page already has the product photo and the facts you would otherwise retype. You spend the time on the script and the actor, not on gathering files.

faq.q: How do I go from a listing link to a finished clip?
faq.a: Paste the link, approve the script, and start the render. You see the credit cost first. There is no separate shoot to schedule before that.

faq.q: How long does the render take?
faq.a: The render runs after you approve the script and the actor. You are not given a stopwatch promise. If it fails, the credits for that job come back.

faq.q: How do I turn a product listing into an ad?
faq.a: Paste the listing, pick a tall or square frame, approve the spoken line, and download. The file has no watermark and can run as an ad.

reviews.h2: How Shops Turn a Product Link Into an Ad
reviews.lead: How ten kinds of sellers start from one public listing. These are examples, not quotes.

items.d: A store seller pastes a public listing, checks the photo and the script, and shows one action of the product.
A gadget seller uses the stand's public page, picks an actor, and asks for one unfolding action so shoppers can see how it opens.
A store running ads takes the same listing, makes one paid post about a single point, and publishes it on Facebook or Instagram.
A social seller pastes the listing again, picks a tall 9:16 size, and posts it to TikTok, Instagram or YouTube Shorts.
A beauty shop lets the page's reviews into the script so the clip mentions what buyers already noticed.
A catalog seller pastes a handful of product links and makes one clip for each item in that sitting.
A wellness seller keeps the same product page and makes a second clip in another language for a new market.
A home shop picks an actor and a voice, then edits one line of the script before downloading.
A small team trims the clip, fixes a caption and swaps the music in the editor. Then they download a file with no logo stamped on it.
A drink seller sends the finished clip to TikTok from the same screen after checking how many credits it will use.
